sql-01.solution: SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE country = 'US'
sql-01.explain: WHERE filters rows before anything is returned.

sql-02.solution: SELECT product_name, unit_price FROM products WHERE category = 'Electronics' AND unit_price > 100 ORDER BY unit_price DESC

sql-03.solution: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM orders GROUP BY status
sql-03.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per distinct status; aggregates are computed per group.

sql-04.solution: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE signup_date IS NULL
sql-04.explain: `= NULL` never matches; NULL requires IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

sql-05.solution: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products, ROUND(AVG(unit_price), 2) AS avg_price FROM products GROUP BY category

sql-06.solution: SELECT c.name, o.order_date FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'completed'

sql-07.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
sql-07.explain: An anti-join: LEFT JOIN then keep rows where the right side is NULL (NOT EXISTS is equivalent and often clearer).

sql-08.solution: SELECT oi.order_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * p.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY oi.order_id

sql-09.solution:
SELECT o.customer_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * p.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY o.customer_id HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * p.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) > 1000
sql-09.explain: WHERE removes non-completed orders row by row; HAVING keeps only groups over the threshold.

sql-10.solution: SELECT emp_name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)

sql-11.solution: SELECT e1.emp_name, e1.department, e1.salary FROM employees e1 WHERE e1.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department = e1.department)
sql-11.explain: A correlated subquery re-evaluates per outer row (engines often rewrite it into a join, but conceptually it is per-row).

sql-12.solution: SELECT product_name, CASE WHEN unit_price >= 300 THEN 'premium' WHEN unit_price >= 50 THEN 'standard' ELSE 'budget' END AS tier FROM products

sql-13.solution: SELECT name, COALESCE(EXTRACT(year FROM signup_date), 0)::INTEGER AS signup_year FROM customers

sql-14.solution: SELECT customer_id FROM orders UNION SELECT customer_id FROM accounts

sql-15.explain: The classic 'latest row per key' pattern, also the heart of deduplication.

sql-16.solution: SELECT emp_name, department, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM employees

sql-17.solution:
WITH r AS (SELECT emp_name, department, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_name) AS rn FROM employees)
SELECT emp_name, department, salary FROM r WHERE rn <= 2

sql-18.solution:
SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date,
  order_date - LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS days_since_prev FROM orders

sql-19.solution:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity * p.unit_price * (1 - oi.discount)) AS revenue
  FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY o.customer_id)
SELECT customer_id, ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue FROM rev WHERE revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM rev)

sql-20.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT emp_id, emp_name, 1 AS depth FROM employees WHERE manager_id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.emp_id, e.emp_name, t.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN tree t ON e.manager_id = t.emp_id)
SELECT emp_name, depth FROM tree

sql-21.solution: SELECT month, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total FROM monthly_sales WHERE region = 'EMEA'

sql-22.solution:
SELECT region, month, revenue,
  ROUND((revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month)) * 100.0 / LAG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly_sales

sql-23.solution: SELECT region, month, ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg FROM monthly_sales

sql-24.solution: SELECT region, month, ROUND(revenue * 100.0 / SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY region), 1) AS pct_of_region FROM monthly_sales

sql-25.solution: SELECT event_type, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users FROM web_events WHERE event_type IN ('login','view','add_to_cart','purchase') GROUP BY event_type

sql-26.solution:
WITH g AS (SELECT user_id, event_ts, LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS prev FROM web_events)
SELECT user_id, SUM(CASE WHEN prev IS NULL OR event_ts - prev > INTERVAL 30 MINUTE THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS sessions FROM g GROUP BY user_id

sql-27.solution:
SELECT customer_id, name, email FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM stg_customers) WHERE rn = 1

sql-28.solution: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM stg_customers GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
sql-28.explain: The simplest and most valuable data-quality test: uniqueness of the key.

sql-29.solution:
SELECT f.sale_id, d.city FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_customer_scd2 d
  ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id AND f.sale_date BETWEEN d.valid_from AND d.valid_to
sql-29.explain: Point-in-time joins are how a warehouse reports history accurately.

sql-30.solution: SELECT customer_id, city FROM dim_customer_scd2 WHERE is_current

sql-31.solution: SELECT customer_id, MAX(updated_at) AS max_updated FROM stg_customers WHERE updated_at > TIMESTAMP '2024-02-01 00:00:00' GROUP BY customer_id
sql-31.explain: A watermark stores the highest timestamp already processed so each run only picks up what is new.

sql-32.solution: SELECT txn_id, account_id, amount FROM transactions WHERE txn_type = 'debit' AND ABS(amount) > 5000

sql-33.solution: SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS txn_total FROM transactions GROUP BY account_id

sql-34.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'cancelled')
sql-34.explain: A join would multiply rows when a customer has many matching orders, forcing a DISTINCT; EXISTS avoids that.

sql-35.solution: SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' AND order_date >= DATE '2024-03-01' AND order_date < DATE '2024-04-01'
sql-35.explain: Naming columns lets columnar storage skip the rest; a sargable date range lets the engine prune data instead of wrapping the column in a function.

sql-36.solution:
WITH oc AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(oc.n, 0) AS orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN oc ON oc.customer_id = c.customer_id
sql-36.explain: Joining the large table row-by-row then grouping is wasteful; reducing it first shrinks the join input.
